Zero-bloat Postgres queue. One SQL file to install, pg_cron or pg_timetable to tick.
Death spiral of a SKIP LOCKED queue under sustained load — the failure mode PgQue avoids by construction

The trade-off is **end-to-end delivery latency** — the gap between `send` and when a consumer can `receive` the event. PgQue ticks **10 times per second** (every 100 ms) by default, so the wait for the next tick is about half the tick period on average. A committed benchmark (`benchmark/tick-rate/`) measures median end-to-end delivery around 52 ms at the default 100 ms tick, with a max of roughly one tick period (about 105–145 ms across the committed runs), plus the consumer's poll interval. The `send` / `receive` / `ack` calls themselves are individually fast. See docs/latency-and-tuning.md for the full breakdown.

3. **End-to-end delivery** — `send` → consumer visibility. About half the tick period on average (default 100 ms tick), measured at a median around 52 ms in the committed `benchmark/tick-rate/` benchmark. Tunable from 1 ms to 1000 ms via `pgque.set_tick_period_ms(ms)`. Does not grow with load.
See docs/latency-and-tuning.md for the breakdown, tick-cadence trade-off table, and comparison with UPDATE/DELETE-based designs.
|Shared-log fan-out: each consumer sees every event|✅|✅|❌|❌|❌|⚠️|

- **PgQ** is the Skype-era queue engine (~2007) PgQue is derived from. Same snapshot/rotation architecture, but requires C extensions and an external daemon (`pgqd`) — unavailable on managed Postgres. PgQue removes both constraints.
- **Que** uses advisory locks (not SKIP LOCKED) — no dead tuples from *claiming*, but completed jobs are still DELETEd. Brandur's bloat post was about Que at Heroku. Ruby-only.
- PlanetScale (2026) — death spiral at 800 jobs/sec with OLAP on the side.

**Requirements:** Postgres 14+, and something that calls `pgque.ticker()` periodically. With `pg_cron`, `pgque.start()` schedules a single 1-second `pg_cron` slot that internally re-ticks every **100 ms (10 ticks/sec)** by default — see Tick rate for tuning. `pg_cron` is pre-installed or one-command available on all major managed Postgres providers (RDS, Aurora, Cloud SQL, AlloyDB, Supabase, Neon); on self-managed Postgres, follow the pg_cron setup guide. Any external scheduler (system `cron`, systemd, a worker loop in your app) works as an alternative — see below.
> `devel/sql/`. The steps below install the stable version.

The `--clientname=pgque` flag is required; pg_timetable only executes chains whose `job_client_name` matches the running worker's client name. Keep that worker running; unlike `pg_cron`, pg_timetable is an external scheduler process, not a Postgres extension background worker. See the pg_timetable docs for production service setup.

- **Idle queues are cheap.** The 100 ms default is the *check cadence*, not a promise to write 10 ticks/sec forever. With no producer writes, most ticker calls return `NULL`; PgQue backs off toward `ticker_idle_period` (default 1 minute), so inactive queues produce occasional metadata writes rather than a steady tick stream. Continuous WAL cost applies only to queues that actually materialize ticks every period. See docs/latency-and-tuning.md for caveats and tuning guidance.

**pg_cron in a different database.** `pg_cron` runs jobs in one designated database (`cron.database_name`, typically `postgres`). If your PgQue schema lives in a different database, use the cross-database pattern to call `pgque.ticker_loop()`, `pgque.maint_retry_events()`, and `pgque.maint()` across databases. *Todo: a future release will detect this and emit the correct `cron.schedule_in_database` calls from `pgque.start()` automatically.*

**Scheduler log hygiene.** Every `pg_cron` job execution writes a row to `cron.job_run_details`, with no built-in purge. PgQue's internal sub-second loop does **not** make this worse — there is still only **one** `pg_cron` slot per second per job, regardless of `tick_period_ms`, so the per-second row count is the same as a 1 tick/sec schedule. Across PgQue's four scheduled jobs (ticker every 1 s, retry every 30 s, maint every 30 s, rotate_step2 every 10 s), those rows accumulate on top of any other pg_cron jobs and grow forever unless you intervene. Prefer a PgQue-specific purge job; disable `cron.log_run` globally only if you do not need successful-run history for any pg_cron jobs. See Latency and tick tuning for the purge recipe. *(Independent issue: `pg_cron` itself has no per-job log toggle as of 1.6.)* If you use pg_timetable, monitor and purge pg_timetable's own execution history tables according to its retention policy; PgQue does not manage those logs.
For existing installs, follow the SQL-file upgrade procedure in docs/installation.md. To uninstall: `\i sql/pgque_uninstall.sql`.

|`pgque_reader`|Consumers, dashboards, metrics, debugging|Read-only info (`get_queue_info`, `get_consumer_info`, `get_batch_info`, `version`, `select` on all tables) **and** the consume API (`subscribe`, `unsubscribe`, `receive`, `ack`, `nack`) plus the underlying PgQ primitives (`next_batch*`, `get_batch_events`, `finish_batch`, `event_retry`, `register_consumer*`, `unregister_consumer`) and the experimental cooperative consumer functions.|

|`pgque_writer`|Producers|The produce API (`send`, `send_batch`) and the underlying primitive (`insert_event`). Does **not** inherit `pgque_reader` — a producer-only role cannot ack/finish/inspect consumer batches.|

|`pgque_admin`|Operators, migrations|Member of both `pgque_reader` and `pgque_writer`, plus full schema/table/sequence access. `uninstall()` is revoked from both `pgque_admin` and PUBLIC (superuser-only — it drops the schema).|

**Roles are global, not per-queue.** A `pgque_reader` granted to an app can ack any consumer's batch and read any other consumer's active batch payloads. Do not grant `pgque_reader` to mutually untrusted applications sharing one database unless you add your own schema-level or database-level isolation. See docs/reference.md — Roles scope for details and recommended isolation patterns.

Aragon Court is a dispute resolution protocol that runs on Ethereum. It's one of the core components of the Aragon Network.
After a long research and development phase, Aragon Court's v1 implementation has been released and deployed.

**Full description of the mechanism: Mechanism documentation**

Aragon Court attempts to find what the subjective truth is with a Schelling game). Jurors are asked to vote on the ruling that they think their fellow jurors are more likely to vote on. To incentivize consensus, jurors that don't vote on the consensus ruling have some tokens slashed. Jurors that vote with the consensus ruling are rewarded with ruling fees and juror tokens from the jurors that voted for a minority ruling.

The basic concept of this project Food Waste Management is to collect theexcess/leftover food from donors such as hotels, restaurants, marriage halls, etc and distribute to the needy people .

The User module is designed for people who wish to donate their excess or leftover food to help reduce food wastage.The User module is responsible for accepting food donations from users who have excess food, such as marriage halls, restaurants, or individuals.The module provides users with the ability to register, login, and donate food. Users can select the type and quantity of food they want to donate, and the system will match their donation with the nearest needy people or organizations.The module also allows users to view their donations.The User module provides the information to the Admin module for further processing.

The Administrator module is for trusts, NGOs, and charities that are registered on the platform. The Admin module is designed for system administrators who manage the food distribution process. The Admin module receives information about the food donation from the User module and lists it for NGOs and charities to choose from.Admins can view and manage the list of donations received, including the type and quantity of food donated. NGOs and charities can select the food donation they need from the Admin module and request a pickup to the Delivery module.The Admin module is responsible for tracking the requests and keeping track of which organizations have taken which donations

The Delivery Person module is for individuals who wish to participate in the food donation process by providing pickup and delivery services. Delivery personnel can register themselves on the platform .The Delivery Person module provides pickup and drop-off services for NGOs and charities who have requested a food donation.The Delivery Person module shows the pickup location and drop location of the food donation.

Overall, the Food Waste Management System is designed to efficiently manage excess food and ensure that it is distributed to those in need. The User module accepts food donations, the Admin module lists them for NGOs and charities to choose from, and the Delivery Person module provides pickup and drop-off services. This system benefits the community by reducing food waste and helping those in need

|**Project memory (own corpus)**|Plugin's own SQLite store (`memories.db`), hard-split from upstream — no shared storage, no compatibility duty. Project identity auto-derived (`git:<root-sha>` / `dir:<hash>`); injected into the m[0] baseline and served to `ctx_memory` for read/write; historian facts auto-promote; FTS 0.7 / vector 0.3 hybrid retrieval|

|**Local vector lane**|MiniLM embeddings run locally via the bundled onnxruntime-web WASM backend — no native build, no API keys; the model download is pinned by revision + sha256 (mirror fallback), cached in the plugin data dir; retrieval candidates get inline + maintenance-tick backfill; any failure fails open to full-text search|

|**m[0]/m[1] memory baseline**|A synthetic notice node carries the frozen baseline plus incremental lanes (`<new-memories>` / `<memory-updates>` / `<user-profile>`); each lane keeps its own watermark, so new memory never rebuilds the cached prefix — unchanged content produces zero diff|

|**Global domains + user profile**|machine/org domains: **staging can be automated** (maintenance tick, LLM classification), **publishing is always human** (approval cards, `/ctx-global approve`); the user profile's render / collect / review are separate switches|
|**Maintenance tick (MC dreamer slice)**|Every 30 min: TTL archiving → batched LLM verify (keep / update / archive) → vector backfill → global-domain candidate staging|

|**Reversible context reclaim**|Tool results get `§N§` tags; `ctx_reduce` **only queues** — drops land in the execute band as `[dropped §N§]` placeholders referencing the originals; `ctx_expand` restores the original text. The cached prefix is never busted spontaneously|

|**Pressure scheduling**|Persistent usage (incl. cache reads/writes) → pressure score → execute/defer decisions (65% threshold, 5 min cache TTL, 85% force band); `CONTEXT_WINDOW_EXCEEDED` triggers emergency reclaim + retry; tiered reduce-guidance nudges|

|**Historian (out-of-band digest)**|One LLM call replays the real prefix (KV cache preserved) → four-tier p1–p4 summary + facts/events, **writes the store only, never touches the wire**; published in the execute band as a `[compacted §C<n>§]` range replacement; `/ctx-recomp` redoes compacted history in place|

|**Compaction seam**|`registerCompactionEngine` can take over `ctx.compaction` (real `compaction/start\|summary\|replace\|end` protocol); **off by default** — the host compaction-basic stays in place|

|**UI integration**|Settings card on the Plugins page (volatile fields, save = live); `shell.overlay` telemetry badge + capsule panel (live metrics + operation record); `session-notice` rows in the session stream; Chinese/English instant switching|
